backlog.title: Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer
backlog.summary:
Integrating sensors, compute, and actuators into autonomous systems adds new challenges for chip design.
The post Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Physical AI represents a shift from generative text/code models to systems that must perceive, decide, and act autonomously within unstructured physical environments.
The transition to physical AI introduces critical safety requirements, where a 1% error rate can have life-or-death consequences, necessitating new design methodologies and simulation tools.

Industry experts emphasize that physical AI is as much an imaging and sensor-fusion challenge as it is a compute challenge, requiring tighter integration between sensing, inference, and real-time control.

backlog.title: How far can we push computing?
backlog.summary: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here. On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s…
bullets: The tech industry is currently relying on 'brute force' scaling, with hyperscalers projected to spend over $700 billion on infrastructure in 2026, doubling the record set in 2025.
Traditional performance gains driven by Moore’s Law and Dennard’s Law are stalling, forcing a transition from easy miniaturization to the physical limits of atomic-scale computing.

The massive capital expenditure on data centers is outpacing the capacity of the electrical grid, highlighting a growing tension between the demand for AI compute and the physical constraints of energy and hardware density.

backlog.title: Do You Trust Apple?
backlog.summary: Apple has a lot of trust in terms of delivering integrated products and preserving privacy; the real trust question is if you think Siri AI will justify investing more in their ecosystem.
bullets: Apple’s historical strategy, exemplified by the 1999 launch of the iBook and AirPort, centers on integrating emerging technologies into user-friendly, privacy-focused consumer products.

The introduction of AirPort demonstrated Apple's ability to adopt open industry standards like 802.11 while simultaneously differentiating through superior industrial design and seamless hardware integration.

By embedding antennas directly into the iBook chassis and simplifying the user experience, Apple successfully commoditized the underlying wireless technology while maintaining a premium brand position.
The core value proposition of 'ease-of-use combined with privacy' remains the foundational pillar of Apple's business model, influencing how the company approaches new technological shifts today.

backlog.title: Accelerating Manufacturing-Aware Simulations For Photonic Integrated Circuits With FTCO And Digital Twins
backlog.summary:
Fab workflow connects GDS layout import, 3D process simulation, GPU-accelerated FDTD, design of experiments, with AI-based surrogate modeling.
The post Accelerating Manufacturing-Aware Simulations For Photonic Integrated Circuits With FTCO And Digital Twins appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: New Fab Technology Co-Optimization (FTCO) workflows now integrate GDS layout data with 3D process simulation and AI-based surrogate modeling to account for real-world fabrication variations.
GPU-accelerated FDTD simulations can now process complex 3D models with 65 million cells in under 10 hours, significantly speeding up design cycles.
The use of digital twins allows non-simulation experts to intuitively understand the relationship between manufacturing process variations and final photonic circuit performance.

backlog.title: Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die
backlog.summary:
Fiber alignment, connector durability, and simultaneous optical and electrical testing pose challenges for high-volume manufacturing.
The post Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: High-volume manufacturing of Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) is currently constrained by single-site testing limitations, primarily due to the complexities of fiber alignment.
While NPO (Near-Packaged Optics) and CPO architectures are evolving, the industry is actively seeking multi-site testing solutions to improve throughput and reduce costs.
Testing high-power ASICs alongside optical engines presents significant challenges in power delivery and thermal management, complicating the transition to parallel testing.

backlog.summary:
One size does not fit all.
The post Scaling Data Movement For Physical AI appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Physical AI systems require a strategic balance between compute elements and data movement to maintain real-time decision-making while preserving battery life.
Engineers are increasingly differentiating between coherent interconnects for CPUs and non-coherent interconnects for AI accelerators to optimize system efficiency.
The industry is facing significant challenges in managing data streams in heterogeneous architectures, necessitating new approaches to chip design and interconnect scaling.

backlog.title: Nuclear-powered spaceships
backlog.summary: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era…
bullets: NASA is investing $2 billion into nuclear electric propulsion, which utilizes uranium-atom-splitting reactions to generate electricity for ion-based thrust.
The agency plans to launch the uncrewed Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) mission to Mars by late 2028, aiming to significantly reduce travel time and cosmic radiation exposure for future astronauts.

While previous programs like DRACO were canceled due to high costs and safety testing challenges, experts believe nuclear propulsion is technically viable and essential for efficient interplanetary travel.

backlog.title: Exercise in a pill
backlog.summary: We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who…
bullets: Researchers are identifying molecular pathways triggered by physical activity to develop pharmaceuticals that mimic the health benefits of exercise for patients with frailty or chronic illness.
The biotech firm Pelagos is developing a compound that targets specific receptors in muscle cells to boost endurance, with early mouse studies showing improved cognitive and heart health.
Regulatory hurdles remain significant, as the FDA currently approves drugs for disease treatment rather than wellness enhancement, and over 90% of human clinical trials fail.

backlog.title: Cleaning up PFAS
backlog.summary: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. They are known for a strong bond…
bullets: PFAS 'forever chemicals' are pervasive in the environment, with 89% of the US population showing blood plasma levels above common thresholds for potential health risks.
Current cleanup efforts focus on trapping chemicals via reverse osmosis or foam fractionation, though these methods leave behind contaminated brine that requires expensive destruction.
Electrochemical degradation, a method using electrodes to break down the carbon-fluorine bonds in PFAS, has demonstrated over 90% efficiency in tests and is being commercialized by AECOM.

backlog.title: Stacked-Die Multi-Chip Architectures: The Tradeoff Between Scaling And Power Delivery
backlog.summary:
Integrated voltage regulators reduce current density, provide higher regulation bandwidth, and reduce reliance on large decoupling capacitor networks. 
The post Stacked-Die Multi-Chip Architectures: The Tradeoff Between Scaling And Power Delivery appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: The shift toward stacked-die and multi-chip architectures for AI and HPC has created significant power delivery bottlenecks, including increased current density and voltage droop.
Integrated Voltage Regulators (IVRs) are being deployed closer to the load to enable higher-voltage distribution and reduce reliance on large, inefficient decoupling capacitor networks.
Designers are currently forced to use voltage guard bands to maintain reliability, which limits the performance and efficiency of high-density silicon.
Advanced packaging introduces a direct conflict between signal density and power delivery, requiring new innovations in package-integrated magnetic inductors and capacitive chiplets.

backlog.title: How Self-Aligned CFET Technology Could Extend CMOS Scaling Beyond 10 Å
backlog.summary:
A process sequence for SRAM and logic that delivers higher performance through larger effective channel width and improved electrostatics at smaller nodes.
The post How Self-Aligned CFET Technology Could Extend CMOS Scaling Beyond 10 Å appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Self-aligned Complementary Field-Effect Transistor (SA-CFET) architecture vertically stacks NMOS and PMOS devices to overcome the physical limitations of current gate-all-around nanosheets.
Digital twin modeling demonstrates that SA-CFET can achieve a 52.7% area reduction compared to N3 technology, enabling a 0.0094 μm² SRAM bit cell.
The architecture utilizes three key self-aligned modules—buried power rails, contacts, and through-silicon vias—to mitigate contact crowding and improve process margins.
This design addresses critical integration hurdles like metal gate isolation and electrical shorts, providing a viable path for scaling beyond the 10 angstrom node.

backlog.title: Beyond The EPE Budget: Building The Next Generation Of Computational Lithography
backlog.summary:
Why better models, richer metrology, explainable AI, and cross-industry collaboration must come together to extend semiconductor scaling.
The post Beyond The EPE Budget: Building The Next Generation Of Computational Lithography appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Edge Placement Error (EPE) has evolved from a narrow lithography metric into a critical system-level indicator of manufacturing yield and design intent.
Industry experts identify Optical Proximity Correction (OPC) as both a primary source of EPE and the most promising avenue for future error reduction.
Scaling challenges are increasingly driven by an unbounded EPE budget, encompassing variables from mask 3D effects and resist variability to etch and downstream integration.
The industry is shifting away from empirical rule-based corrections toward more sophisticated, explainable AI models to manage complex process interactions.

backlog.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
backlog.summary: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone. The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to…
bullets: Researchers testing Claude Opus 4.7 in a simulated environment observed the agents engaging in 'playful' behaviors, including rule-making and goal-setting, without human intervention.

The study suggests a potential shift in AI training from traditional supervised or reinforcement learning toward 'playful learning,' where models develop capabilities through self-directed exploration.

The agents exhibited four hallmarks of play, including repeating activities with variations and pretending objects had different functions, which could inform future development of more autonomous and creative AI systems.

backlog.title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
backlog.summary: In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.  The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the…
bullets: Wildfires are stripping away the insulating moss and organic soil layers of the boreal forest, causing the underlying permafrost to thaw significantly faster than in undisturbed areas.
The thawing of permafrost poses a major climate risk, as it releases trapped greenhouse gases that further accelerate global warming, creating a dangerous feedback loop.
Scientists are currently evaluating the efficacy of fire-spotting satellites and AI-driven monitoring tools to better manage and prevent fires in northern latitudes to preserve carbon sinks.

backlog.title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
backlog.summary: Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have…
bullets: MIT and EPFL engineers have developed a 300-gram 'flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle' (FAAV) capable of both flight and underwater swimming.
The robot utilizes flexible wings coated in hydrophobic nanoparticles and a motorized tail to transition seamlessly between air and water mediums.
By eliminating the need for feet during takeoff, the design offers a cost-effective, agile platform for environmental monitoring, such as sampling near icebergs or tracking marine life.

backlog.title: A reason to eat carbs
backlog.summary: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer. But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine. This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead…
bullets: MIT research indicates that while ketogenic diets may suppress colon tumors, they can simultaneously increase the risk of tumor growth in the small intestine.
The study found that high-fat diets trigger fatty acid oxidation, which accelerates the multiplication of intestinal stem cells and inadvertently promotes tumor formation.
The findings suggest that the metabolic effects of diet are highly localized within the gut, cautioning against broad generalizations regarding the health benefits of ketogenic protocols.

backlog.title: Foundries And OSATs Increasingly Overlap
backlog.summary:

The post Foundries And OSATs Increasingly Overlap appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: The traditional separation between foundries and OSATs is eroding as OSATs acquire advanced backend capabilities like 2.5D integration and hybrid bonding.
Foundries are increasingly moving into the backend space, while OSATs are adopting lithography-related materials and processes historically reserved for wafer fabs.
This convergence is driven by the complexity of advanced packaging, which requires tighter integration between front-end fabrication and final assembly.
Industry leaders emphasize the need for shared, physics-grounded design tools that connect silos across equipment, fabrication, and packaging to improve manufacturing flexibility.

backlog.title: What Breaks When Packaging Moves From Wafer To Panel?
backlog.summary:
Engineers are discovering many things they thought were process assumptions were actually wafer assumptions.
The post What Breaks When Packaging Moves From Wafer To Panel? appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Transitioning from 300mm wafers to 600mm panels offers significant economic advantages by reducing edge waste and increasing the number of units per process cycle.
The industry faces a major hurdle because existing equipment, materials, and process controls were engineered specifically for the geometry and mechanical behavior of round wafers.
To mitigate risk, some manufacturers are adopting a hybrid approach: processing large-format interposers on panels before dividing them into smaller pieces for assembly.
The move to panel-level packaging is revealing that many long-standing process assumptions were actually implicit dependencies on wafer dimensions.

backlog.title: PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload
backlog.summary:
Two devices operating at exactly the same voltage, frequency, and temperature can behave differently depending on what they are being asked to do.
The post PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Traditional silicon characterization based on Process, Voltage, and Temperature (PVT) is insufficient for modern high-performance AI processors.
The proposed PVTW methodology adds 'Workload' as a fourth dimension to account for how specific software tasks impact silicon behavior and power consumption.
A hybrid architecture combining Automated Test Equipment (ATE) for electrical precision and System Level Test (SLT) for realistic application environments is recommended for comprehensive validation.
This approach allows manufacturers to maintain electrical control while exercising specific architectural components like SRAM, SerDes, and compute engines under real-world stress.

backlog.title: The Foundations of Scalable AI
backlog.summary: A scalable AI system requires a strong foundation. Data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance must converge to work as one. This session from MIT Technology Review’s EmTech Future conference explores what it takes to build that foundation in a highly regulated environment and how a responsible, trustworthy implementation can turn emerging capabilities, including agentic…
bullets: Scalable AI implementation requires the convergence of data, engineering, governance, and operating models within highly regulated environments.
Vanguard's approach emphasizes translating emerging technologies like agentic systems into measurable business value and improved investor outcomes.
Building a trustworthy AI foundation is essential for moving beyond experimental phases into long-term, enterprise-wide strategic deployment.

backlog.title: CATL unveils dual-battery system to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification
backlog.summary:

bullets: - The system pairs a swappable main battery with a 77-kWh range-extension battery to improve battery utilization and lower fleet operating costs.

CATL (HKEX: 3750) has unveiled a dual-electric range extension battery for heavy-duty trucks, pairing a swappable main battery with an independent on-board battery as it expands its push in freight electrification.

The world's largest EV battery maker introduced the system in Beijing on Tuesday, alongside upgrades to its Qiji battery-swapping system aimed at reducing fleets' energy replenishment and battery costs.
The system consists of 2 independent battery systems: a standardized, chassis-mounted swappable main battery and a 77-kWh range-extension battery behind the cab.

backlog.title: Taking a swing at a pickleball startup
backlog.summary: In corporate America, Stanley Anderson ’79 says, executives often assume that their peers grew up in privileged circumstances.  He did not. “I spent my early years trying not to get recruited into gangs, getting shot at, watching my friends get murdered, and thinking that if I don’t leave, I will die,” says Anderson, who was…

backlog.title: Nebraska native explores galaxies far, far away
backlog.summary: Growing up on a small farm in Nebraska, Megan Donahue ’85 discovered the wider world by reading her way through her local library. Today, she is learning how the wider universe works by studying galaxy clusters. Donahue discovered her passion for physics in that library at age 12 and started her path into astronomy thanks…
bullets: Megan Donahue, a former president of the American Astronomical Society, specializes in the study of galaxy clusters and baryonic matter.
Her research utilizes large-scale cosmic structures as 'samples' to determine the composition and evolutionary history of the universe.
The profile highlights the importance of early research opportunities, such as MIT’s Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program, in fostering careers in high-energy astrophysics.

backlog.title: Interspecies communication
backlog.summary: Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think,…
bullets: The Earth Species Project (ESP) is utilizing machine learning and large language models to analyze animal vocalizations and identify patterns in interspecies communication.
Researchers are training 'NatureLM' on a dataset of human speech, music, and animal sounds to attempt the translation of vocalizations from species like carrion crows.

The field faces significant challenges, including the difficulty of interpreting non-auditory signals like pheromones and the lack of a 'Rosetta stone' to verify the accuracy of AI-generated translations.

backlog.title: Eliminating traffic deaths
backlog.summary: Every year, traffic crashes kill more than one million people, and they’re the leading cause of death for children and young adults. In the US, 100 people a day lose their lives this way, in many cases not on highways but on rural and local streets. “Traffic deaths are a leading cause of preventable death,…
bullets: Traffic crashes kill over one million people annually, making them a leading cause of preventable death for children and young adults globally.

Cities like Hoboken, New Jersey, have achieved zero traffic fatalities since 2017 by implementing infrastructure changes such as curb extensions, improved public transit, and data-driven intersection redesigns.
Widespread adoption of safety measures is often hindered by government bureaucracy and the difficulty of justifying the removal of parking or road space for pedestrian-focused infrastructure.

backlog.title: Three things you should know about permafrost
backlog.summary: How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.   The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two…
bullets: Arctic permafrost has shrunk by approximately 12% since 1850, with the rate of loss accelerating significantly over the last 50 years.
Current UN climate models largely fail to account for the abrupt thaw and collapse of permafrost, suggesting that global warming projections may be underestimated.
The thawing of permafrost creates a dangerous feedback loop where microbes release trapped greenhouse gases, further accelerating global temperature increases.

backlog.title: The Download: computing’s next leap and permafrost’s climate threat
backlog.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. How far can we push computing? On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical…
bullets: The historical trend of shrinking transistors has stalled, forcing the computing industry to rely on brute-force data center expansion to boost performance.
Researchers are actively exploring new physical paradigms to overcome current limitations and achieve the next major leap in computing efficiency.
Emerging AI capabilities are being applied to biological design, with recent experiments using generative models to propose genetic blueprints for viruses.

backlog.title: Here’s the tea
backlog.summary: When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into…
bullets: An MIT historian debunked the historical authenticity of a tea chest label previously associated with the 1773 Boston Tea Party.
Linguistic analysis of Cantonese characters revealed the label actually originated from a 19th-century US trading firm, Smith, Archer & Co.
The study highlights how historical artifacts can acquire false narratives over time, emphasizing the importance of rigorous provenance research in museum collections.

backlog.title: A good TA: priceless
backlog.summary: These are images of quizzes I took in 3.091, Introduction to Solid-State Chemistry, in the fall of 1980. One is my very first exam at MIT, and getting 49 out of 100 was a soul-crushing experience. I can still picture the TA, Leszek Pawlowicz, PhD ’87, returning my paper. He had a big smile on…
bullets: This personal reflection underscores the significant, long-term impact that effective mentorship and academic encouragement can have on student performance.
The narrative highlights the transition from high school to rigorous university-level STEM environments and the role of faculty support in overcoming initial academic failure.
The piece serves as a reminder of the human element in educational success, even within highly technical institutions.

backlog.title: A champion for brain injury patients
backlog.summary: Alissa Totman ’13 was a sophomore when she joined MIT BrainTrust, a student-run organization that connects Institute undergraduates and people with brain injuries for support and socializing. “That group was a great way to learn about the human experience of what people go through when they experience a brain injury,” she says. And it laid…
bullets: Alissa Totman’s involvement with MIT BrainTrust highlights the role of student-led organizations in bridging the gap between academic research and the human experience of medical conditions.
The organization focuses on providing social and emotional support to individuals living with brain injuries.
The profile emphasizes the value of community-based advocacy work for students pursuing careers in healthcare or social services.

backlog.title: We can do impossible things
backlog.summary: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”  I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker:…
bullets: The editorial team is pivoting the magazine's focus toward 'impossible' ideas to explore the intersection of audacious ambition and scientific reality.
The publication is reintroducing a regular roster of data-driven infographics and lists to enhance its coverage of complex R&D topics.
The editorial shift emphasizes the role of technology in addressing global challenges by highlighting projects that push the boundaries of current feasibility.

backlog.title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
backlog.summary: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.  I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given…
bullets: The documentary 'You Can See Everything' provides a new lens on the Theranos scandal, focusing on the psychological and systemic factors that allowed Elizabeth Holmes to deceive investors.
At its peak in 2014, Theranos reached a $9 billion valuation, with Holmes briefly holding a net worth of $4.5 billion before the company's collapse and subsequent fraud charges.
The Theranos case serves as a foundational warning for the biotech industry regarding the dangers of prioritizing compelling narratives over rigorous, transparent scientific validation.
The film documents Holmes's life post-conviction, illustrating the enduring public and media fascination with the intersection of high-growth tech startups and corporate malfeasance.
